newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Coffee industry eyes big growth potential in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Coffee industry eyes big growth potential in Asia.

text.p: Asian countries, with booming populations and low market shares in a traditionally tea-drinking region, are catching the eye of the international coffee industry with their potential for demand growth.

Leading industry officials, traders, roasters and producers, meeting in Vienna at an International Tea and Coffee Symposium conference last week, all agreed even modest growth rates in Asia would be of importance.

"Coffee traditions in South East Asia have always existed, but the consumption was low because of a poor purchasing power. Now there is an increased demand for better quality coffees in Asia as the purchasing power has increased," according to Ong Siong Kai, managing director of Singapore-based commodity traders Hiang Kie Pte Ltd.

"There is a very good future market for coffee in Asia," said Urs Brunner, managing director of Boncafe Thailand, which processes and trades coffee in the Asian markets of Thailand, Singapore and Hong Kong.

"Asia is very good at picking up food trends from the U.S., you have already fast food chains all over Asia and once the marketing is done right....there will be a growth in coffee consumption in Asia," said Brunner.

Boncafe, a Swiss-Thai joint venture concentrating on the gourmet coffee markets, has run roasting factories in Singapore and Hong Kong for several years already, and more recently set up facilities in Thailand.

"The habit of drinking coffee is coming up now in Thailand after being well-established in Singapore and Hong Kong for years. In Singapore and Hong Kong you can find coffee shops all over the cities now," Brunner told Reuters.
Silvano Corsini, president of top Italian roaster Caffe Corsini, saw strong growth opportunities in Japan.

"There is a very strong future market in Japan. It's a rich market, they want high quality and there is a lot of growth potential. Over the past three years the volume of our sales to Japan has doubled every year, now we sell 100 tonnes of coffee a year to Japan," Corsini said.
Industry officials from Peru, which exported some 90,000 tonnes of mild washed arabica coffee in the 1996/97 crop year, said 25 percent of total exports went to South Korea and Japan.

"Korea is a new consumer market, we first started exports to Korea three years ago, but already Korea makes up 10 percent of all our exports," said Eduardo Montauban Urriaga of Peru's biggest exporters' association, Camara Peruana de Cafe.

In Indonesia local consumption has grown steadily over several years and has reached an annual level of 120,000 tonnes, according to Mansyur Tandiono, a senior official with the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters.

"Per capita consumption is only 0.70 kg per year and from here it's very easy to increase the consumption. In Singapore they already drink a lot of coffee and the local consumption in countries like Thailand is increasing a lot.

"We are seing consumption increasing in Indonesia year by year with some 5-10 percent. I think it would be realistic to see local consumption in Indonesia increasing a lot more," Tandiono told Reuters.
The market which remained on the lips of everyone attending the conference was China.
"Of course everyone is eagerly looking at China because of the huge market size," said a leading European trader.

"We have seen all these markets opening up in Japan, Korea and Singapore, coffee is regarded as a chic product by the younger generation -- now it's already starting in China with small-scale imports of coffee," he told Reuters.

"China, with 1.2 billion people, has a per capita consumption of only about 0.004 kg a year, but even if the figure is small, because of the population, you are talking about many thousands tonnes of coffee," said Tandiono.

Singapore's Ong Siong Kai said, "It's not easy to make people change habits overnight, in China they are still tea drinkers and it's only near the southern coastal areas that you find the buying power.
"... I definitely think China should be able to double their consumption within three to five years," he added.
